title: Navigation and communication between screens
subtitle: Make push, presentation, saving, cancellation, and containment behave deliberately.
objectives: Choose navigation stacks, tabs, and modal presentations by user intent.
Pass data forward and return changes through callbacks or delegates.
Keep cancellation separate from saving an edited draft.
Use the required view-controller containment sequence.
prerequisites: Days 2–5: ownership, lifecycle, layout, and form input.
A UIKit app with a UINavigationController at the scene root.
Understand that copying a value can represent an isolated editing draft.

sections.title: Use containers to express the app's structure
body: UINavigationController manages a stack: pushing moves deeper into a hierarchy and popping returns to the previous screen. The navigation bar reflects the top controller's title and items. UITabBarController switches between peer destinations such as Tasks and Settings; each tab can own its own navigation stack. Do not use a tab for a one-time action such as Save.

A modal presentation begins a focused flow, such as adding a task or selecting a filter. Dismissal returns to the presenting context. A screen presented modally is not automatically inside a navigation controller, so wrap it in one if it needs a navigation bar with Save and Cancel. Decide whether the user is moving deeper into content or temporarily entering a task, then choose the container that communicates that relationship.

sections.title: Pass required data at construction time
body: If a detail screen cannot function without an identifier or task value, require that input in its initializer for programmatic construction. This makes an invalid unconfigured screen harder to create. Storyboard-based screens often receive data before the segue finishes; document that configuration point and avoid force-unwrapped properties that fail much later during view loading.

Pass a model value or stable identifier, not a UILabel copied from the source screen. Views belong to a hierarchy; domain data belongs to the feature. A value draft is useful for editing: changing the draft does not immediately mutate the list's displayed source. On Save, return the validated result; on Cancel or Back, discard the draft. Preserve the task's stable identifier when editing rather than treating every save as a new entity.

sections.title: Return changes through an explicit contract
body: A closure works well for one or two simple results such as onSave(TaskItem). A delegate protocol works well for a named multi-event relationship that benefits from a documented contract. Notifications fit broad observations where the sender should not know every observer, but are usually harder to trace than a direct callback for one parent-child edit flow.

Pay attention to ownership. A parent may retain or present an editor, so a callback stored by the editor should normally capture the parent weakly. A child delegate pointing to the owning parent should be weak and class-bound. UI callbacks should execute on the main actor; do not let a background notification or service callback directly mutate UIKit. Make the result contract tell callers whether the value was merely edited, validated, or actually persisted.

sections.title: Presentation has its own lifecycle and cancellation rules
body: Modern sheet presentations can have detents and may be dismissed interactively. A Cancel button is only one path out of a modal. Decide whether an unsaved draft may be discarded by swiping, whether you need a dismissal delegate to ask about changes, or whether a critical flow should temporarily prevent interactive dismissal with isModalInPresentation. Do not block dismissal reflexively for every form.

Use the correct inverse operation: pop a pushed controller; dismiss a presented controller or its presentation container. Calling popViewController on a modal that has no navigation controller does nothing. Avoid triggering a new presentation repeatedly from appearance callbacks. Wait for the current transition to complete when coordinating multi-step navigation, and keep route decisions in one clear place as the app grows.

sections.title: Child controllers need full containment
body: Adding another controller's view as a subview does not establish proper controller containment. A custom container should call addChild, insert and constrain the child's view, then call child.didMove(toParent:). This informs UIKit about the relationship so lifecycle forwarding and other behavior can work correctly.

To remove a child, call willMove(toParent: nil), remove its view, and call removeFromParent. The latter completes the parent-removal relationship. Do not use custom containment when a standard navigation or tab controller already matches the design. Coordinators can later centralize navigation policy; they are a way to organize responsibilities, not a requirement for every two-screen app.

example.title: Edit a title, save it back, or cancel with Back
walkthrough: Add both classes to the UIKit target and set the scene root to UINavigationController(rootViewController: TaskHomeViewController()). The initializer is programmatic; this editor is not designed for storyboard decoding.
Tap Edit. The current title is passed by value through the editor's initializer, so the original screen has valid data before editing begins.
Change the text and tap Back. Nothing calls onSave, so the original title remains unchanged.
Edit again and tap Save. Validation succeeds, the callback updates the parent, and the editor pops itself.
The callback captures the parent weakly. This example updates in-memory screen state only; saving to a repository and handling failure will be added later.
example.expectedOutput: A task title with an Edit button. Back discards edits; Save updates the original title and returns. Empty or overlong titles show inline feedback and do not leave the editor.

exercises.title: Create two peer tabs
exercises.prompt: Write a function that creates a tab bar with Tasks and Settings destinations, each using its own navigation controller.
requirements: Give each tab a title and SF Symbol.
Do not use a tab item as a Save action.
hints: A navigation controller is itself a view controller.
exercises.explanation: Each tab preserves its own stack while the user switches peer destinations. Use this function's return value as the scene window's root controller; do not wrap the entire tab controller in another unnecessary navigation stack.
checks: Each tab has its own navigation bar.
Switching tabs does not create a new root each time.
Editing in Tasks does not push a screen onto Settings.

exercises.title: Present a cancellable sheet
exercises.prompt: Create a simple help controller and present it as a sheet inside a navigation controller. Provide a Done button that dismisses the presented flow.
requirements: Use dismiss rather than pop for the modal flow.
Avoid retaining the controller through its own stored action.
hints: Configure the sheet on the presented navigation controller.
The controller's navigation bar can hold a Done UIAction.
exercises.explanation: The navigation controller is presented modally, so dismiss ends the flow. This help screen has no unsaved state, making interactive dismissal reasonable. Add content as an extension exercise; the solution focuses on presentation behavior.
checks: The sheet displays a navigation bar and Done item.
Done returns to the original presenter.
Dragging to the large detent does not create another controller.

exercises.title: Implement correct child containment
exercises.prompt: Write a helper that embeds a child controller inside a dedicated container view belonging to the parent, and a helper that removes it.
requirements: Constrain the child view to all container edges.
hints: The container must already be in the parent's view hierarchy.
exercises.explanation: Controller ownership and view hierarchy must agree. Merely inserting child.view skips the relationship UIKit uses for appearance forwarding and other container behavior. Use standard containers unless a custom one is actually required.
checks: The child's parent property is the expected controller after embedding.
The child fills the container when it resizes.
After removal, the child has no parent and its view has no superview.

quiz.question: Which operation usually reverses a push?
quiz.explanation: A navigation controller owns the stack and pops the top pushed controller.

quiz.question: Why pass an editing draft as a value?
options: It separates tentative edits from committed source data.
quiz.explanation: The caller can commit on Save and discard on Cancel without leaking partial edits into the original data.

quiz.question: A child editor stores a callback that updates its parent. What capture is usually appropriate?
options: A strong capture with no ownership analysis.
A weak parent capture when the parent owns or presents the editor.
An unowned capture because callbacks never outlive screens.
quiz.explanation: The weak backward reference avoids forming an ownership cycle and safely handles a vanished parent.

quiz.question: What does a modal editor need if it should show a navigation bar?
options: Nothing; every modal has one automatically.
A UINavigationController wrapper or another intentional container.
quiz.explanation: A plain UIViewController does not automatically receive a navigation bar when presented.

quiz.question: Which is the correct addition sequence for custom containment?
options: didMove, then addChild, then remove the view.
addChild, add/constrain the child's view, then didMove(toParent:).
quiz.explanation: This sequence establishes the controller relationship and its view hierarchy with the required lifecycle notification.

pitfalls: Using pop for a modal or dismiss for an ordinary pushed detail can produce confusing behavior.
Passing UIKit views as data entangles screen hierarchies.
A strong callback to an owning parent can retain the whole flow.
Interactive sheet dismissal is a cancellation path that needs an explicit unsaved-draft policy.
Adding a child controller's view without containment skips essential UIKit relationships.
checkpoint: Explain why a feature uses push, tab, or modal presentation.
Demonstrate Save versus Back cancellation without accidental mutation.
Show the ownership graph of a parent, editor, and callback.
Embed and remove a child using the full sequence.
State whether a returned edit is merely validated or durably saved.

references.title: Apple — Implementing a container view controller

capstone.title: Connect list, editor, and settings
steps: Create a task-list root and push a task editor with required input.
Return a validated draft through a weakly captured callback.
Keep Back and Cancel from mutating source data.
Add Settings as a peer tab only if it is a genuine destination, and document modal dismissal behavior.
